subject: Critical Thinking
title: Bayes' Theorem: Updating Beliefs with New Evidence
description: A quick, practical guide to Bayes' Theorem: Updating Beliefs with New Evidence.

hook.text: A medical test is 99% accurate. You test positive for a disease that affects 1 in 10,000 people.

buildup.text: Bayes' Theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). It calculates how to update prior beliefs with new evidence.

discovery.text: The prior matters enormously. If the disease is rare, even an accurate test produces mostly false positives.

twist.text: Most people ignore the base rate and focus on the test accuracy. Doctors make this error with real patients.

climax.text: Bayesian thinking is the mathematically correct way to learn from evidence.

punchline.text: Don't just ask how strong the evidence is.

quiz.question: Why does a 99% accurate test often produce false positives for rare diseases?
options: When the prior probability is very low, even small false positive rates dominate

details.summary: Bayes' theorem is a formula for updating probability estimates when new evidence arrives. It combines your prior belief with the likelihood of the evidence to produce a revised posterior belief.
details.whyItMatters: Bayes' theorem is the mathematically correct way to change your mind. It prevents both ignoring new evidence and overreacting to it.
takeaways: Prior probability plus new evidence yields posterior probability
The strength of evidence determines how much beliefs should shift
Bayesian updating prevents both stubbornness and gullibility

faq.question: Can you explain Bayes' theorem with a simple medical example?
faq.answer: If a disease affects 1% of a population and a test is 90% accurate, a positive result does not mean 90% certainty. Bayes' theorem shows the actual probability is only about 8% because the low base rate must be factored in.

faq.question: How can Bayesian thinking be applied without doing formal calculations?
faq.answer: Start with an estimate of how likely something is, then ask how strongly new evidence supports or undermines it. Shift your confidence proportionally to the evidence strength. Even informal Bayesian reasoning improves judgment.
